deployment.notes: No build step — upload the files and you're done. Any host that serves files works.

components.notes: Nothing beyond where the files live and the domain name.

cost.notes: The tooling costs nothing; you only pay for hosting and the domain (~$1/mo averaged).

0.security: Smallest possible attack surface: no server code, no dependencies to patch. Main risks are leaked hosting credentials and any third-party scripts you paste in.

scalability.notes: Traffic scales as well as your host does. What doesn't scale is authoring — shared headers/footers get copy-pasted into every page past ~10 pages.

0.grc: Few concerns. Add a privacy notice if you add analytics or forms, and keep license notices for any copied CSS/JS.
0.auditing: Run an HTML validator and a broken-link checker before each upload; check pages with Lighthouse for accessibility.
0.costMonitoring: Nothing to monitor here — the cost lives with the hosting choice.
0.performance: Excellent by default: no framework JavaScript to download. Optimize images and you'll score near-perfect.

deployment.notes: One build command produces a folder of files. Most hosts run the build for you on every git push.

components.notes: Adds a git repo, which most hosts connect to for automatic builds.

cost.notes: Generators are open source. Build minutes are free at this size on every major host.

1.security: Output is still plain files, so the live site has almost nothing to attack. Build-time npm/gem dependencies can carry supply-chain risk — pin versions and use Dependabot.

scalability.notes: Serves any traffic a CDN can. Builds slow down past a few thousand pages (Hugo stays fast; Jekyll gets slow).

1.grc: Check the theme's license if you use one. Same privacy-notice needs as any site that adds analytics or forms.
1.auditing: Fail the build on broken internal links (most generators have a plugin), and use the host's deploy previews to review changes before they go live.
1.costMonitoring: Watch the host's build-minute usage if you rebuild very often; otherwise nothing.
1.performance: Excellent — output is pre-rendered HTML with little or no JavaScript.

deployment.notes: A build step plus framework config (static export mode, image handling, base paths). More things can break between versions.

components.notes: A git repo connected to the host for automatic builds, with a larger npm dependency tree to keep updated.

cost.notes: Free tooling. Build times are longer, but still well within free build minutes for small sites.

2.security: The live site is still static, but the dependency tree is hundreds of npm packages. Keep them updated and avoid exposing secrets in client-side environment variables.

scalability.notes: Serves any traffic. The main benefit is that you can later switch to server rendering without rewriting components.

2.grc: Watch for framework features that quietly assume a server or a specific vendor (e.g. image optimization) — it's a lock-in risk, not a compliance one.
2.auditing: Add a few component tests plus a link checker in CI; compare Lighthouse scores before and after framework upgrades.
2.costMonitoring: Nothing beyond hosting. Watch for accidentally using features that need a paid server runtime.
2.performance: Very good, but ships more JavaScript than a plain generator. Astro ships near-zero JS by default; Next.js ships React's runtime.

deployment.notes: Push to a branch or run a GitHub Actions workflow; HTTPS and custom domains are built in.

components.notes: Code and hosting live in the same account.

cost.notes: Free for public repos. Private-repo Pages needs a paid GitHub plan (~$4/mo).

0.security: Free HTTPS. Turn on 2FA for GitHub — whoever controls the repo controls the site. No custom security headers (e.g. CSP) are possible.

scalability.notes: Soft limits: ~100 GB/month bandwidth and a 1 GB site size. Not meant for commercial, high-traffic sites.

0.grc: GitHub's terms discourage using Pages mainly for commercial transactions. Content in a public repo is visible to everyone.
0.auditing: The Actions log shows each deploy; every change is a git commit, so you get a full audit trail automatically.
0.costMonitoring: Nothing to monitor — no usage billing.
0.performance: Good: served from GitHub's CDN. Less control over caching than Netlify/Vercel.

deployment.notes: Connect a git repo; every push builds and deploys, and every PR gets a preview URL.

components.notes: Built-in forms and functions can replace other services if you need them later.

cost.notes: Free tier covers most small sites. Pro is ~$19 per team member per month once you need more.

1.security: Free HTTPS, configurable security headers, and password-protected deploy previews on paid plans.

scalability.notes: Global CDN. The free tier has bandwidth/build-credit limits; past them the site pauses or you upgrade.

1.grc: Netlify is a US company; check its DPA if visitors are in the EU. Free-tier usage is subject to fair-use terms.
1.auditing: Deploy log and one-click rollback to any previous deploy; deploy previews let someone review before merging.
1.costMonitoring: Set usage notifications in team settings — overages (bandwidth, form submissions, function calls) are where surprise bills come from.
1.performance: Excellent for static files; fast global CDN with sensible cache defaults.

deployment.notes: Connect a git repo; every push builds and deploys with preview URLs. Especially good support for Next.js.

components.notes: Built-in analytics and serverless functions are available as add-ons.

cost.notes: The Hobby plan is free but non-commercial only. A business site needs Pro (~$20 per member per month).

2.security: Free HTTPS, configurable headers, deployment protection for previews. Keep team access tight — anyone with access can deploy.

scalability.notes: Global edge network handles traffic spikes easily; usage-based billing above the included amounts.

2.grc: The Hobby plan's non-commercial rule is a compliance issue in itself for a business site. Check the DPA for EU visitors.
2.auditing: Deployment history with instant rollback; preview URLs per branch for review.
2.costMonitoring: Enable spend management and set a hard spending cap on Pro — function or bandwidth overages are the usual surprise.
2.performance: Excellent; fast edge CDN with framework-aware caching.

deployment.notes: Usually FTP/SFTP upload or a script you write; no automatic deploy on git push unless you set it up.

components.notes: On a VPS you also own the operating system and web server.

cost.notes: Shared hosting runs ~$3–10/mo; a small VPS ~$5–12/mo. Intro prices often double on renewal.

3.security: On a VPS, you must patch the OS, harden SSH, and renew certificates yourself. Shared hosting is patched for you but shares a server with strangers.

scalability.notes: One server in one region. Fine for normal traffic; a viral spike can take it down without a CDN in front.

3.grc: You choose the data-center region, which helps with data-residency requirements. On a VPS, keeping the server patched is your responsibility.
3.auditing: Keep the site in git and deploy from it, rather than editing on the server, so you always know what's live. Add uptime monitoring.
3.costMonitoring: Fixed monthly price — put the renewal date on the calendar, since renewal price hikes are common.
3.performance: Good in the server's region, slower far away. Put a free CDN (e.g. Cloudflare) in front for global visitors.

deployment.notes: Nothing to deploy.

components.notes: No extra accounts.

cost.notes: No cost.

0.security: No third-party script on your pages — nothing that could be compromised to inject code.

scalability.notes: Not applicable — nothing to scale.

0.grc: Simplest compliance position: no tracking, no cookie banner needed for analytics.
0.auditing: Your host may still show basic request counts if you need a rough sense of traffic.
0.performance: Best possible — no extra script to load.

deployment.notes: Add one script tag to your page template.

components.notes: One more account to keep paid and secured.

cost.notes: ~$9–15/mo for small traffic; priced by monthly pageviews. Plausible can be self-hosted for free.

1.security: A third-party script runs on every page. Choose a reputable vendor and consider loading it through your own domain.

scalability.notes: The vendor handles scale; cost rises with pageviews.

1.grc: Cookie-free and designed to need no consent banner under GDPR. Still mention it in your privacy notice.
1.auditing: Compare its numbers against your host's request logs occasionally; set up goal tracking to confirm events fire.
1.costMonitoring: Plans are pageview tiers — check usage monthly so a traffic spike doesn't bump you up a tier unexpectedly.
1.performance: Negligible impact: the script is under ~1 KB.

deployment.notes: Add the tag; setting up GA4 events and reports properly takes longer than installing it.

accounts: Cookie-consent tool (if you have EU visitors)
components.notes: Usually also implies a consent-banner service.

cost.notes: Free. A consent-management tool may cost ~$0–10/mo.

2.security: A large third-party script on every page. Grant property access per person, not via shared logins.

scalability.notes: Handles any traffic; data sampling kicks in for very large reports.

2.grc: Uses cookies and personal data: needs a consent banner for EU/UK visitors, a privacy-policy disclosure, and data-retention settings. Some EU regulators have challenged its use.
2.auditing: Use GA4's DebugView to confirm events fire; check that consent mode actually blocks tracking before consent.
2.costMonitoring: Free, but count the time cost of consent management and reporting setup.
2.performance: Adds ~50–100 KB of script; minor but measurable impact on load time.

deployment.notes: Write a Markdown file, commit, push — the host rebuilds and publishes.

components.notes: Posts live in the repo; no separate content system.

cost.notes: Open-source tooling; you only pay for hosting and the domain.

0.security: No admin login to attack — publishing access equals repo access, so protect the git account with 2FA.

scalability.notes: Serves any traffic. Builds slow down past a few thousand posts on some generators (Hugo stays fast).

0.grc: Full ownership of your content in plain files — no vendor lock-in or export problem. Check theme licenses.
0.auditing: Every post change is a git commit (full history). Add a link checker and an RSS validator to the build.
0.costMonitoring: Nothing to monitor beyond the host's build minutes.
0.performance: Excellent — pre-rendered pages with little JavaScript.

deployment.notes: Two systems to wire: the CMS triggers a rebuild through a webhook whenever someone publishes.

components.notes: Plus API keys and a rebuild webhook to manage between them.

cost.notes: Free tiers cover a solo blog. Team features jump fast: Sanity ~$15/seat/mo, Contentful's paid tier is ~$300/mo.

1.security: CMS API tokens must stay server/build-side only. Writers' CMS accounts need 2FA and the least access they need.

scalability.notes: The site still serves static files; CMS API rate limits only matter at build time.

1.grc: Content lives in a vendor's database — check export options and where the data is hosted. Your writers' accounts are personal data held by the vendor.
1.auditing: CMS version history shows who changed what; check that the publish webhook actually triggers a rebuild (failed builds are easy to miss).
1.costMonitoring: Watch seat count, API calls, and asset bandwidth against the free tier's limits.
1.performance: Excellent for readers (static output). Builds take longer because they fetch content over the API.

deployment.notes: Self-hosted means running a server, a database, and updates. Managed hosting removes most of that.

components.notes: Plugins often bring their own vendor accounts and licenses.

cost.notes: Managed WordPress/Ghost runs ~$5–25/mo; premium themes and plugins add more.

2.security: WordPress is the most-attacked platform on the web: plugins and its admin login need constant updates and hardening. Ghost has a smaller attack surface.

scalability.notes: Needs caching or a CDN to survive traffic spikes; database-backed pages are heavier than static files.

2.grc: Comments, newsletters, and member signups collect personal data — needs a privacy policy and data-deletion process. Plugin licenses vary.
2.auditing: Turn on automatic security updates, use an activity-log plugin, and test backups by actually restoring one.
2.costMonitoring: Watch renewal pricing and how plugin subscriptions add up; set billing alerts if self-hosting.
2.performance: Good with caching, slow without it. Heavy themes and plugins are the usual cause of slowness.

deployment.notes: Push to deploy; HTTPS and custom domains included.

components.notes: Code, content, and hosting in one place.

cost.notes: Free for public repos.

0.security: Free HTTPS; protect the GitHub account with 2FA. No custom security headers.

scalability.notes: ~100 GB/month soft bandwidth limit — plenty for most personal blogs.

0.grc: Not for commercial-transaction sites. Drafts in a public repo are publicly visible — keep drafts in a branch or a private repo.
0.auditing: Git history is your audit trail; the Actions log records each publish.
0.performance: Good: GitHub's CDN serves static files quickly.

deployment.notes: Git-push deploys plus preview URLs to review a post before it goes live.

components.notes: Netlify Forms can handle a newsletter signup without another service.

cost.notes: Free tier fits most blogs; Pro ~$19/member/mo.

1.security: Free HTTPS and configurable security headers.

scalability.notes: Global CDN; free-tier bandwidth limits apply.

1.grc: Check the DPA for EU readers, especially if you use Netlify Forms to collect emails.
1.costMonitoring: Set usage notifications — a viral post can exhaust free bandwidth.

deployment.notes: Git-push deploys with previews; best fit if the blog is built with Next.js.

components.notes: Optional built-in analytics.

cost.notes: Hobby is free but non-commercial; a monetized blog needs Pro (~$20/member/mo).

2.security: Free HTTPS, configurable headers, deployment protection.

scalability.notes: Edge network absorbs viral spikes; usage-billed beyond the included amounts.

2.grc: Ads, sponsorships, or paid content count as commercial — that rules out the Hobby plan.
2.costMonitoring: Set a spend cap on Pro.

deployment.notes: No deploy step — write in the browser and click Publish.

components.notes: Newsletter, comments, and memberships are often built in, which avoids extra vendors.

cost.notes: ~$4–25/mo depending on plan; plugins or custom themes often require higher tiers.

3.security: The platform patches and secures everything; you manage the user accounts and 2FA.

scalability.notes: The platform handles traffic; plan tiers may cap members or newsletter sends.

3.grc: Your content and subscriber list live with the vendor — confirm you can export both. The vendor is the data processor for reader emails.
3.auditing: Use the platform's revision history; check that scheduled posts and newsletter sends actually went out.
3.costMonitoring: Price tiers are usually by member/subscriber count — watch the next tier's threshold.
3.performance: Good; managed caching and CDN are included.

deployment.notes: Nothing to deploy.

components.notes: No extra accounts.

cost.notes: No cost.

0.security: No user-generated content, so no spam or abuse to moderate.

scalability.notes: Not applicable.

0.grc: No reader data collected and no moderation obligations.
0.performance: Best — no comment widget to load.

deployment.notes: Add an embed script to your post template.

accounts: Comment service (giscus uses GitHub Discussions; Disqus has its own account)
components.notes: Readers also need an account with that service to comment.

cost.notes: giscus is free. Disqus is free with ads; ad-free plans start ~$11/mo.

1.security: Spam and abuse moderation become your job. The embed is a third-party script on your pages.

scalability.notes: The vendor handles the load.

1.grc: Disqus's free tier serves ads and tracks readers — needs consent handling in the EU. giscus stores comments publicly on GitHub.
1.auditing: Check moderation queues regularly; make sure comments load on a sample of old posts after theme changes.
1.costMonitoring: Free tiers usually stay free; watch for changes to Disqus's plans.
1.performance: giscus is light; Disqus adds noticeable weight from ads and trackers. Lazy-load either below the fold.

deployment.notes: Turns a static blog into an app: an API, a database, migrations, and a server or functions to deploy.

components.notes: Several new services where before there were none.

cost.notes: ~$0–25/mo on free-tier databases and functions; grows with traffic and spam volume.

2.security: You own input sanitization (XSS), spam, rate limiting, auth, and protecting stored emails. This is the riskiest option.

scalability.notes: Depends entirely on what you build; a database-backed write path needs real capacity planning.

2.grc: You become the data controller for reader names and emails: privacy policy, deletion requests, and possibly content-moderation obligations.
2.auditing: Needs automated tests for the API, error monitoring, and checked database backups.
2.costMonitoring: Billing alerts on the database and functions; spam bots can drive up usage-based costs.
2.performance: Depends on implementation; load comments asynchronously so they don't slow the page itself.

deployment.notes: One app, one build, one deploy. Rollback means redeploying the previous version.

components.notes: The smallest set of moving parts.

cost.notes: One small app instance plus a small database; free tiers can cover early use.

0.security: One codebase to secure and one place to apply auth — simplest to reason about. A single vulnerability can expose everything.

scalability.notes: Scales well by adding instances behind a load balancer; scaling individual features separately isn't possible.

0.grc: Easy to document and audit: one system, one data flow. Access control lives in one place.
0.auditing: One test suite and one log stream; add request logging and error monitoring (e.g. Sentry) from day one.
0.costMonitoring: One bill per component; set a billing alert on the hosting account.
0.performance: Fast: in-process function calls with no network hops between parts.

deployment.notes: Deploys exactly like a monolith; the module boundaries are code organization, not infrastructure.

components.notes: The smallest set of moving parts — module boundaries add no infrastructure.

cost.notes: One small app instance plus a small database; free tiers can cover early use.

1.security: One codebase and one place to apply auth, plus clearer ownership of which module touches which data. A single vulnerability can still expose everything.

scalability.notes: Scales like a monolith now, and a module can be pulled out into its own service later if it really needs to.

1.grc: Module boundaries make it easier to show which code touches sensitive data.
1.auditing: Add architecture tests (e.g. dependency rules) so modules can't quietly reach into each other.
1.costMonitoring: One bill per component; set a billing alert on the hosting account.
1.performance: Fast: modules call each other in-process, with no network hops.

deployment.notes: Two deployables that must stay compatible; API changes need versioning or coordinated releases.

accounts: Domain registrar (plus DNS for api.* subdomain)
components.notes: Also CORS settings and an API base URL per environment.

cost.notes: Frontend is often free on a static host; the API and database are ~$5–25/mo.

2.security: CORS, token storage in the browser, and API auth all become explicit concerns. The API is publicly reachable — rate limiting matters.

scalability.notes: Frontend scales on a CDN for free; the API scales independently.

2.grc: Two systems to document; make sure the API's logs don't capture personal data you didn't mean to keep.
2.auditing: Contract tests between frontend and API catch breaking changes; monitor both separately.
2.costMonitoring: Two bills — set alerts on both, especially API egress.
2.performance: Very fast page loads from the CDN; each data fetch adds an API round trip.

deployment.notes: Many services, each with its own pipeline, config, and version — usually needs containers, orchestration, and service discovery.

accounts: Orchestration (e.g. Kubernetes or a managed equivalent)
components.notes: Each service multiplies the operational surface.

cost.notes: Several always-on services, separate databases, and observability tooling add up quickly even at low traffic.

3.security: Service-to-service auth, network policies, secrets per service, and a much larger attack surface.

scalability.notes: Each service scales independently — the main reason to choose it, and rarely needed early.

3.grc: Personal data spread across many stores makes deletion requests and data mapping harder.
3.auditing: Requires distributed tracing and contract tests; a bug may only appear when services interact.
3.costMonitoring: Tag every resource by service and use budget alerts per team/service; idle services still cost money.
3.performance: Network hops between services add latency; usually slower per request than a monolith unless carefully designed.

deployment.notes: Use a managed provider (Neon, Supabase, RDS, Azure) and run migrations as part of each deploy.

components.notes: Plus backup settings and a migration tool (e.g. Prisma, Flyway).

cost.notes: Free tiers exist (Neon, Supabase); small paid instances ~$5–25/mo.

0.security: Never expose the database publicly; use a least-privilege app user, TLS, and parameterized queries (or an ORM) against SQL injection.

scalability.notes: Handles far more than most apps need; read replicas and connection pooling come next.

0.grc: Choose the provider's region for data residency; encryption at rest is standard on managed services. Define a backup retention period.
0.auditing: Database constraints catch bad data; run migrations in CI against a real Postgres; test restoring a backup.
0.costMonitoring: Watch storage growth and compute hours on serverless plans; set billing alerts.
0.performance: Excellent for relational queries with the right indexes; use EXPLAIN on slow queries.

deployment.notes: Use a managed provider (PlanetScale, RDS, Azure) and run migrations as part of each deploy.

accounts: Managed MySQL provider (e.g. PlanetScale, RDS, Azure)
components.notes: Plus backups and a migration tool.

cost.notes: Small managed instances ~$5–25/mo; free tiers are rarer than for Postgres.

1.security: Never expose the database publicly; use a least-privilege app user, TLS, and parameterized queries (or an ORM) against SQL injection.

scalability.notes: Proven at very large scale; read replicas are mature.

1.grc: Choose the provider's region for data residency, confirm encryption at rest, define a backup retention period, and check the vendor's compliance certifications.
1.auditing: Use strict SQL mode so bad data errors instead of silently converting; test migrations and restores.
1.costMonitoring: Watch storage and instance size; set billing alerts.

deployment.notes: Usually MongoDB Atlas; no schema migrations, but data-shape changes still need scripts.

components.notes: Plus IP allow-listing and backup settings.

cost.notes: Free shared cluster for development; dedicated clusters start around $50/mo.

2.security: Never run with auth disabled or open to the internet (a classic breach cause). Watch for NoSQL injection in query filters.

scalability.notes: Scales horizontally with sharding; best when data is naturally document-shaped.

2.grc: Flexible schemas make it easy to store personal data you didn't intend to — define and validate document shapes.
2.auditing: Use schema validation rules; cross-document consistency is easier to get wrong than with SQL joins and constraints.
2.costMonitoring: Watch the cluster tier — the jump from shared to dedicated is a big price step.
2.performance: Very fast for reading whole documents; weaker for complex joins and reports.

deployment.notes: A single file next to the app — but it needs persistent disk, which rules out most serverless hosts.

components.notes: No database service at all (or a hosted variant like Turso).

cost.notes: No database bill; you pay only for the app server's disk.

3.security: No network port to attack. Protect the file with OS permissions and include it in backups.

scalability.notes: One writer at a time on one machine. Great for small/read-heavy apps; hard to run several app instances.

3.grc: Backups are your responsibility — a lost disk means lost data unless you replicate (e.g. Litestream).
3.auditing: Run an integrity check and test backup restores regularly.
3.costMonitoring: Nothing to monitor beyond disk size.
3.performance: Extremely fast for reads on one server — no network hop at all.

deployment.notes: You build sign-up, login, password reset, and email verification — plus an email-sending service.

accounts: Transactional email service (e.g. Postmark, SendGrid, Resend)
components.notes: Users and password hashes live in your own database.

cost.notes: Email services are free or ~$1–15/mo at low volume. The real cost is development and maintenance time.

0.security: Highest risk: password hashing (argon2/bcrypt), session handling, brute-force protection, reset-token flows, and MFA are all on you.

scalability.notes: Scales with your database; no per-user vendor fees.

0.grc: You hold credentials — a breach is a notifiable incident in most jurisdictions. Needs a documented security process.
0.auditing: Log every login, failure, and password reset; test the reset flow end to end; get a security review before launch.
0.costMonitoring: Watch email-sending volume — a bot hammering sign-up or reset can drive it up.
0.performance: Fast; password hashing is deliberately slow (~100 ms) — that's expected.

deployment.notes: Install an SDK, configure redirect URLs per environment, and add login pages from the vendor.

accounts: Auth provider (e.g. Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth)
components.notes: Separate configuration for development and production.

cost.notes: Free up to ~10,000–25,000 monthly active users; paid tiers often jump to $25–$100+/mo, and SSO features cost more.

1.security: The vendor handles password storage, MFA, and breach detection — usually much safer than DIY. You still must verify tokens correctly on the server.

scalability.notes: Scales with the vendor; pricing, not technology, is the limit.

1.grc: The vendor processes user personal data — sign their DPA; most hold SOC 2 / ISO 27001, which helps your own compliance.
1.auditing: Use the vendor's login logs and anomaly alerts; write tests for your token verification and role checks.
1.costMonitoring: Track monthly active users against the free tier threshold — growth can trigger a sudden plan jump.
1.performance: Adds a redirect at login; nothing on normal requests if tokens are verified locally.

deployment.notes: Register an OAuth app with each provider and configure callback URLs per environment.

accounts: Developer accounts with each provider (Google, GitHub, etc.)
components.notes: One OAuth client and secret per provider per environment.

cost.notes: Free.

2.security: No passwords to store. Protect OAuth client secrets and validate the state parameter to prevent CSRF.

scalability.notes: No scaling concern.

2.grc: Users without a Google/GitHub account can't sign in — an accessibility and reach issue. Request only the scopes you need.
2.auditing: Test each provider's login flow after any config change; log which provider each user came from.
2.performance: Adds a redirect to the provider at login only.

deployment.notes: Nothing to deploy.

components.notes: No extra accounts.

cost.notes: No cost.

3.security: Anything the API can do, anyone can do. Only safe if the app holds no private data and has no write actions worth abusing.

scalability.notes: Not applicable — but adding auth later means touching every route.

3.grc: Don't collect personal data without access control. Add rate limiting even without logins.
3.auditing: Make sure no admin or write endpoint is reachable from the public internet.
3.costMonitoring: Unauthenticated endpoints can be abused to drive up usage-based costs — rate limit them.

deployment.notes: Git-push deploys with previews; backend code runs as serverless functions.

components.notes: The database almost always comes from another vendor.

cost.notes: Free to start; commercial use needs Pro (~$20/member/mo), plus the database.

0.security: No servers to patch. Keep secrets in the platform's environment variables, never in client code.

scalability.notes: Scales automatically. Watch database connection limits — many function instances can exhaust them (use pooling).

0.grc: Pick function regions near your database and users; sign each vendor's DPA.
0.auditing: Deploy previews, function logs, and instant rollback; add error monitoring.
0.costMonitoring: Set a spend cap — function invocations and bandwidth are usage-billed.
0.performance: Fast static pages; functions can have cold starts of a few hundred milliseconds.

deployment.notes: You set up the OS, runtime, reverse proxy, TLS, process manager, and a deploy script.

components.notes: You also own OS updates and monitoring.

cost.notes: A small VM ~$5–20/mo — cheap, predictable, and you can run the database on it too.

1.security: You patch the OS, configure the firewall, harden SSH, and renew certificates. Easy to fall behind.

scalability.notes: Scale up by resizing; scaling out needs a load balancer and more manual setup.

1.grc: Full control of the data's location, but also full responsibility for patching and backups.
1.auditing: Keep server configuration in scripts (not hand edits); add uptime and disk monitoring.
1.costMonitoring: Fixed price — but snapshots, extra disks, and bandwidth overages add line items.
1.performance: Consistent, no cold starts; limited to one region unless you add a CDN.

deployment.notes: Push code or a Dockerfile; the platform builds and runs it, with TLS and health checks included.

components.notes: Often one vendor for app and database.

cost.notes: ~$5–25/mo for a small always-on app plus database.

2.security: The platform patches the hosts; you keep your container image's dependencies updated.

scalability.notes: Add instances or regions from the dashboard.

2.grc: Choose regions deliberately; check backup and data-retention options on the managed database.
2.auditing: Deploy history, health checks, and logs; add error monitoring.
2.costMonitoring: Usage-based with fixed-size instances — check the monthly estimate after each scaling change.
2.performance: Consistent, no cold starts on always-on instances.

deployment.notes: Many services to wire together (compute, networking, IAM, database); infrastructure-as-code is strongly recommended.

components.notes: Powerful, but every piece needs configuration.

cost.notes: Easy to land at $30–100/mo for a small app once you add a load balancer, database, and logging; free credits help at first.

3.security: Strongest tools available, but misconfigured IAM roles and public storage buckets are common breach causes.

scalability.notes: Effectively unlimited.

3.grc: Best compliance options (regions, certifications, audit logs) — and the most to configure correctly to actually use them.
3.auditing: Turn on the provider's audit logs (CloudTrail / Activity Log); define infrastructure in code so changes are reviewable.
3.costMonitoring: Set budgets and alerts on day one, tag resources, and review the bill monthly — forgotten resources are the classic surprise.
3.performance: Excellent and tunable, but only as good as your configuration.

deployment.notes: Two codebases, two build pipelines, two app-store review processes. iOS builds require a Mac.

components.notes: Signing keys for both stores must be backed up — losing the Android key can block updates.

cost.notes: Apple charges $99/year (~$8/mo); Google Play is a one-time $25. A Mac and CI build minutes add more.

0.security: Full access to platform security features (Keychain, Keystore, biometrics). Never ship API secrets inside the app — they can be extracted.
